claims.text: The Institute was incorporated and sited deliberately inside a university: 'The IOFP received its certificate of incorporation on September 7, 1955.' 'The plan of the IOFP was to house an institute within an academic institution, so as to avoid the conflict that physicists felt working in an industrial setting. The chosen location was the physics department at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.'

claims.source: History of the Institute of Field Physics (1955-1959), Section II, https://physics.unc.edu/department-history/section-ii/
claims.text: Every piece of the Institute's publicity was to carry a disclaimer, written into its design by John Wheeler. The 'Protection Clause' reads in part: 'The work in field physics and gravitation theory carried on at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and financed by the Institute of Field Physics, as fundraising agency, has no connection with so-called "anti-gravity research" of whatever kind and for whatever purposes.'

claims.source: History of the Institute of Field Physics (1955-1959), Section II, https://physics.unc.edu/department-history/section-ii/
claims.text: Martin money reached the Institute directly: Trimble and the Glenn Martin Company 'purchase[d] a "Founder's Membership" for the Institute of Field Physics, for the considerable sum of $5000, they also offered their support to solicit further funding'. The same source records that Louis Witten 'was the first researcher hired by RIAS, of the Glenn Martin Company', and identifies the Glenn L. Martin Company as 'now Lockheed-Martin'.

claims.source: History of the Institute of Field Physics (1955-1959), Section II, https://physics.unc.edu/department-history/section-ii/
claims.text: Air Force money and Air Force logistics reached it through a named laboratory: Joshua Goldberg, 'in charge of aspects of the Air Force's funding of general relativity, in the "modern physics research branch" (based at the Aeronautical Research Laboratory at Wright Patterson Air Force Base)', gave a $5,000 grant and secured Military Air Transport Service flights for conference participants from eleven nations.

claims.source: The Role of Gravitation in Physics: Report from the 1957 Chapel Hill Conference, eds. Dean Rickles and Cecile M. DeWitt, Edition Open Sources, Sources 5, 2011, https://edition-open-sources.org/sources/5/index.html
claims.text: The 1957 Chapel Hill conference was the Institute's inaugural event: 'In January 1957, a group of physicists from several countries met at the University of North Carolina to discuss the role of gravitation in physics ... The Chapel Hill conference also marked the establishment of the Institute of Field Physics, directed by Bryce and Cecile DeWitt. The conference was the inaugural conference of this institute.'

desc: The Institute of Field Physics received its certificate of incorporation on 7 September 1955 and was placed inside the physics department at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, directed by Bryce and Cecile DeWitt and funded principally by the Winston-Salem industrialist Agnew Bahnson. Its inaugural event was the Conference on the Role of Gravitation in Physics at Chapel Hill in January 1957, now known as GR1. It sits on the same money as the board's existing Martin thread: George Trimble and the Glenn L. Martin Company bought a Founder's Membership for $5,000 while the company was separately standing up RIAS, whose first researcher was Louis Witten. The thing a node must carry is what the Institute wrote about itself. On John Wheeler's insistence a 'Protection Clause' was attached to every IOFP publicity statement declaring that the work 'has no connection with so-called "anti-gravity research" of whatever kind and for whatever purposes', and the department's own history says the instruction to avoid anti-gravity connotations runs through the founding correspondence like a mantra.
